claims.text: A quaternary equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloy will transition from dislocation-glide-dominated strain-rate sensitivity to strain-rate-insensitive yielding as temperature increases.
The transition occurs when the activation energy for dislocation climb exceeds the available thermal energy.
The proposed behavior requires retention of a single-phase FCC structure without competing phase transformations.
The initial alloy is a homogeneous, fine-grained, high-dislocation-density FCC solid solution without secondary phases or precipitates.
Tensile tests will span strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1 and temperatures from 77 K to approximately 0.5 Tm.
Dislocation cell structures and wavy dislocation configurations facilitate cross-slip and climb at elevated temperatures.
Cross-slip and dislocation climb become rate-limiting deformation steps at elevated temperatures.
At low temperatures, plasticity is governed by dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
Low-temperature dislocation glide and twinning produce high yield-strength sensitivity to strain rate.
Increasing temperature causes a transition to diffusion-controlled dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding.
In the elevated-temperature regime, deformation is limited by atomic diffusion rather than dislocation mobility.
Diffusion-controlled deformation causes yield strength to become insensitive to further increases in strain rate.
Yield strength versus strain rate will have a steep positive slope at low temperature and a zero-slope plateau at elevated temperature.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi exhibits increased strength and ductility at cryogenic temperatures because of deformation-induced twinning.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi transitions from dislocation glide at 800 K to diffusion-controlled dislocation creep at 1000 K.
The hypothesis fails if strain induces an FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC transformation, or if precipitation or melting destroys solid-solution stability.
The transition temperature depends on the stacking-fault energy and diffusion coefficients of the particular quaternary alloy.
Trace oxygen or impurities can form oxide precipitates that alter dislocation pinning and mask intrinsic strain-rate insensitivity.
Observation of an FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC transformation during deformation would identify TRIP rather than diffusion-controlled creep as the operative mechanism.
A constant, high activation volume is characteristic of glide, whereas a decrease is characteristic of diffusion-controlled deformation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis places the transition at a temperature where the activation energy for climb exceeds the available thermal energy, implying climb cannot be activated. The mechanism and mediator fields instead say that increasing temperature activates diffusion-controlled climb and that wavy dislocations indicate crossing the thermal barrier.
